newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela banks need still better capitalization.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela banks need still better capitalization.

text.p: Venezuela's banking system, only recently recovered from the 1994-95 financial crisis, needs to further increase capitalization levels if it is to keep up with growing credit demand, Central Bank president Antonio Casas Gonzalez said, El Nacional reported.

Although bank intermediation -- which describes the amount banks lend per each bolivar deposited -- has risen to 44 percent from 34 percent at the end of 1994, regulations currently limit banks from placing loans worth more than 10 percent of bank equity with one client.
"That's leading large companies to seek syndicated loans, or foreign financing," Casas said Thursday in a banking seminar in western oil town Maracaibo, El Nacional reported.
"That trend can only be reversed by (Venezuelan banks) increasing their paid-in capital to meet increasing credit demand from the real economy."

Casas said banks had nearly doubled their capitalization rates -- the ratio of shareholders' equity to total assets (such as loans and investments) -- to 12.9 percent from 6.9 percent at the end of 1994.

But while industry figures show total bank loans outstanding are now some $5.4 billion, loan demand is expected to increase as economic recovery sets in. State-owned oil giant Petroleos de Venezuela's 10-year plan envisions annual investment of some $6 billion alone.
Casas added that continuing increases in bank supervision were also required, although the financial crisis, that swallowed some $11 billion in bail-outs five years ago, was fully over.
